                                   3                                           LEGAL STANDARD

                                   4            Under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 12(b)(6), a district court must dismiss a complaint

                                   5   if it fails to state a claim upon which relief can be granted. To survive a Rule 12(b)(6) motion to

                                   6   dismiss, the plaintiff must allege “enough facts to state a claim to relief that is plausible on its

                                   7   face.” Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544, 570 (2007). A claim is facially plausible when

                                   8   the plaintiff pleads facts that “allow the court to draw the reasonable inference that the defendant

                                   9   is liable for the misconduct alleged.” Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662, 678 (2009) (citation

                                  10   omitted). There must be “more than a sheer possibility that a defendant has acted unlawfully.” Id.

                                  11   While courts do not require “heightened fact pleading of specifics,” a plaintiff must allege facts

                                  12   sufficient to “raise a right to relief above the speculative level.” Twombly, 550 U.S. at 555, 570.

                                  15   plaintiff. See Usher v. City of Los Angeles, 828 F.2d 556, 561 (9th Cir. 1987). However, the court

                                  16   is not required to accept as true “allegations that are merely conclusory, unwarranted deductions of

                                  17   fact, or unreasonable inferences.” In re Gilead Scis. Sec. Litig., 536 F.3d 1049, 1055 (9th Cir.

                                  18   2008).

                                  19            If the court dismisses the complaint, it “should grant leave to amend even if no request to

                                  20   amend the pleading was made, unless it determines that the pleading could not possibly be cured

                                  21   by the allegation of other facts.” Lopez v. Smith, 203 F.3d 1122, 1127 (9th Cir. 2000). In making

                                  22   this determination, the court should consider factors such as “the presence or absence of undue

                                  23   delay, bad faith, dilatory motive, repeated failure to cure deficiencies by previous amendments,

                                  24   undue prejudice to the opposing party and futility of the proposed amendment.” Moore v. Kayport

                                  25   Package Express, 885 F.2d 531, 538 (9th Cir. 1989).

                                       Stay Discovery [Dkt. No. 28]. Although I GRANT the Motion to Dismiss, I do so with leave to
                                  28   amend. Because ongoing discovery may be useful in helping plaintiffs to narrow the scope of
                                       their case, the Motion to Stay Discovery is therefore DENIED.

                                   1                                             DISCUSSION

                                   2          I.      UWM Disclosure and Plaintiff Consent

                                   3          UWM argues that the plain language used in the Terms of Use and Privacy Policy

                                   4   “expressly disclosed” to plaintiffs the type of information obtained via customer use of UWM’s

                                   5   website and its dissemination to third-parties, including technology companies. Mot. 5. Its

                                   6   argument is bolstered by its reference to the Privacy Policy’s explanation of UWM’s use of

                                   7   “cookies” and its “Social Media and Third Party Links” provision. The Privacy Policy defines a

                                   8   “cookie” as “a small file that is assigned by the web server to your computer. The use of cookies

                                   9   allows UWM to identify which pages of the site are accessed. That information is then used to

                                  10   improve the Website and your online experience.” The Privacy Policy also contains a “Social

                                  11   Media and Third Party Links” provision. That provision is reproduced in full below:

                                  22          over third-party websites.

                                  23   Privacy Policy at 6.

                                  24          It is challenging to square plaintiffs’ admission that they entered into contract with UWM

                                  25   via the Terms of Use and Privacy Policy with their allegations that they did not consent to UWM’s

                                  26   use of their “personal and financial information.” See FAC ¶ 74 (“The contracts that UWM has

                                  28   Contracts’).”). The only specific information that plaintiffs allege UWM shares to third parties is

                                   6   third-parties, but that plaintiffs consented to its sharing and therefore cannot now bring an action

                                   7   alleging they did not. Mot. 4–8.

                                   9   Oppo. 5. See Shah v. Capital One Financial Corp., 768 F. Supp. 3d 1033, 1044 (N.D. Cal. 2025)

                                  10   (Thomspon, J.) (“Because the issue of whether Plaintiffs consented to Defendant’s disclosure of

                                  11   their personal information is a factual question, the Court need not reach it at the motion to

                                  14   reasonable person understood that an action would be carried out so that their acquiescence

                                  16   assert: “Consent is a disputed factual issue here. Defendants say Plaintiffs consented, and

                                  17   Plaintiffs say they did not. Thus, consent is not a sufficient basis to dismiss this case now.” Oppo.

                                  18   8.

                                  20   Policy and Terms of Use with UWM, see FAC ¶ 74, nor do they allege that they did not agree to

                                  21   the contents of those self-described contracts. At only one point in the complaint, not referenced
